advisor.summary: The classic sole-proprietor structure: the spouse works as a bona fide W-2 employee, and the business adopts a written §105 plan covering employees and their families. Because family coverage picks up the owner as the employee's spouse, household medical costs — premiums, deductibles, dental, vision — become Schedule C deductions that cut income tax and SE tax alike, a layer the §162(l) deduction never touches. Rev. Rul. 71-588 blesses the architecture; the litigation turns entirely on whether the spouse's employment is genuine, with Shellito and Haeder marking the two ends of the proof spectrum. With the spouse as the sole participant, the plan rests inside the §9831(a)(2) exemption from the ACA market reforms. The engine deducts reimbursed medical costs against Schedule C profit, so the modeled delta already captures the SE-tax layer.
mechanics: The spouse performs genuine services for the Schedule C business as a W-2 employee, and a written plan reimburses medical expenses of employees, their spouses, and dependents — the family definition that pulls the owner's own costs into the plan.

Reimbursements of §213(d) expenses are excluded from the spouse's income under §105(b), escape FICA, and are deducted on Schedule C — shrinking net earnings from self-employment and, with them, the SE-tax base.
Rev. Rul. 71-588 remains the controlling administrative blessing of the spouse-employee, family-coverage structure.

For the same dollars, the design beats §162(l): the self-employed health insurance deduction is income-tax-only and premiums-only, while the §105 plan converts premiums plus out-of-pockets into business deductions carrying SE-tax savings — never claim the same premium under both.

With fewer than two current-employee participants, the plan is exempt from the ACA market reforms under §9831(a)(2); hiring non-family employees ends that exemption and forces a §105(h) eligibility analysis.
The engine models the reimbursement as a Schedule C deduction capped at business profit; the spouse's wage cost belongs to the spouse-payroll strategy and is not double-counted here.

authority.note: Excludes employer reimbursements of the employee's, spouse's, and dependents' medical expenses — the family sweep that carries the owner.
Defines an accident or health plan: it must be a plan for employees; it need not be insured, but it must exist before benefits are paid.
The controlling ruling: a sole proprietor's spouse-employee covered under the business medical plan; reimbursements — including for the owner as a family member — excludable and deductible.
The business deduction for plan reimbursements, and the premiums-only, income-tax-only alternative the plan outperforms — never both on the same dollars.
Exempts plans with fewer than two current-employee participants from the ACA market reforms.
Self-insured nondiscrimination rules — live the moment non-family employees are kept out of the plan.
Defines the medical expenses the plan may reimburse.

The bona fide employment battleground: the Tax Court first disallowed where the spouse had done identical work unpaid for years; the Tenth Circuit vacated, and the deductions ultimately survived — the proof file decides these cases.
Denied a plan resting on paper-only spousal employment: no real duties, no records, no wages actually paid.

requirements: A Schedule C or farm proprietorship — the structure fails for S corporation families because >2% shareholder attribution reaches the spouse.
Bona fide employment: genuine duties, contemporaneous time records, and reasonable W-2 wages actually paid through payroll (Forms 941, 940, W-2).
A written plan adopted before any reimbursement, covering employees and their families, with an annual cap.
Real reimbursement mechanics — the spouse submits receipts, the business account pays, and a log is kept.
If other employees exist, the plan covers them per its terms and §105(h) testing applies.
risks: Bona fide employment is the entire exam: Shellito v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2010-41 shows the government pressing hardest where the spouse's duties predate the payroll, and Haeder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2001-7 shows paper-only employment losing outright — time records, genuine duties, and wages actually paid decide these cases.
A plan document adopted after reimbursements begin protects nothing — pre-adoption payments are simply taxable.
Non-family employees change the economics: excluding them invites §105(h) discrimination taxation; covering them raises the cost of every reimbursement dollar.
The owner cannot participate directly — a proprietor is not their own employee; every benefit must flow through the spouse's employment.
Claiming the same premiums under both the plan and §162(l) is a recurring preparer error.
stateNotes: Conformity: the Schedule C deduction and the spouse's exclusion both ride the federal computation into any state that starts from federal AGI.
PTET: no PTET interaction — Missouri's and most states' pass-through entity taxes reach S corporations and partnerships, not Schedule C proprietorships.
Missouri: conforms through RSMo §143.121; the reduced Schedule C profit flows straight onto the Missouri return with no addback.
reviewChecklist: Employment file complete: job description, time log, benchmarked wage, payroll filings current.
Plan document executed and dated before the first reimbursement; annual cap set.
Reimbursement log ties every receipt to a business-account payment.
No §162(l) claim on premiums flowing through the plan.
Participant count still within the market-reform exemption; §105(h) analysis refreshed if employees were added.

client.teaser: Your family's medical bills can become business deductions — cutting self-employment tax too.
client.headline: Turn family medical bills into business deductions
plainEnglish: If you run your own unincorporated business and your spouse truly works in it, the business can adopt a medical plan for its employees and their families. Your spouse is the employee. The family is you and your kids.

So bills your family already pays — premiums, deductibles, dental, vision, copays — can be repaid by the business and deducted. This deduction also cuts your self-employment tax, which most health write-offs cannot touch.

It has to be real. Your spouse must truly work and get real paychecks, and the written plan must exist before any money moves. Done right, the IRS has accepted this setup for over fifty years. Done sloppy, it is the first thing an auditor pulls apart. We do the paperwork right.
client.analogy: Most families pay medical bills after tax takes its bite. Here, the business pays them first — before the income-tax bite and before the self-employment-tax bite.
benefits: Family medical bills become business deductions
Cuts self-employment tax on top of income tax
Covers what insurance misses — deductibles, dental, vision
A setup the IRS has recognized for decades
steps: WE document your spouse's real role and set up proper payroll.
WE put the written plan in place before any money moves.
YOU have your spouse turn in the family's medical receipts; the business repays them from its account.
WE take the deduction and keep the file audit-ready.
clientCommitments: Your spouse truly works the hours — and logs them
Every repayment has a receipt and comes from the business account
Tell us before you hire anyone else — it changes the plan's rules

annualMaintenance: Refresh the employment file: hours log, duties, wage reasonableness
